textContent.text: Prince Hal rolled out of bed, stumbling around the dark room. Today was the day of the royal parade, and he needed to get dressed quickly. His father was expecting him at sunrise, and Hal did not want to disappoint him. Hal hoped that this early meeting meant that he was ready for more royal tasks.
As Hal rushed to throw his shoes on, he remembered all the times his parents had to wait for him. What would his father say if Hal was late again?
Hal rushed out of the castle. The sky was beginning to lighten, so he knew he needed to take the shortcut in order to make it in time.

Hal darted past shopkeepers setting out baskets, and villagers calling, "Good morning!" Just before he arrived at the parade grounds, he stopped. A villager's wagon lay on its side. Vegetables and packages were scattered across the road. The villager's children rushed to gather their belongings while the villager struggled to lift the wagon back upright.
Hal knew the sun would appear any minute. His parents were probably already waiting by the field.
Then Hal remembered something his father often said: "Kindness is the greatest crown you can wear."

Without another thought, Hal stepped forward. He grabbed one side of the wagon and pushed with all his might. It slowly flipped back onto its wheels. Then, Hal began collecting the family's belongings. Following the lead of their prince, others nearby began to help, too. Soon the mess was cleared, and the tired family went on their way, smiling.
Hal thanked those who pitched in, and then looked up. Rays of sunlight spilled across the rooftops. His heart sank. He was late.

Her little ship shot away from the huge Mothership. Soon, all she could see was the enormous Planet SHIN-E and its hundreds of little moons. Now, she just had to find mega-gold.

textContent.text: Bella knew that her job was especially important today. The Mothership used mega-gold to power its kitchens, and it was running out. Without it, everyone would be stuck eating tasteless food goop.

Bella steered her ship between the moons, zooming past each one. But Bella couldn't find mega-gold anywhere. After passing several more moons with no luck, she started sweating. It never took this long to finish her scouting work!
Her eyes burned from staring into the endless black. Every moon looked the same.
Tired and grumpy, she called her friend Luna. Luna appeared on Bella's screen.
"Bella!" said Luna, her curly dark hair bouncing. "How's it going out there?"
"Bad," said Bella. "I can't find mega-gold anywhere! I don't want to do this anymore."
"You should give up immediately and come home. Food goop isn't so bad," said Luna.
Bella's mouth hung open. She hadn't expected that! "Ew, no!" she cried.

want to give up?" asked Luna, smiling.

textContent.text: Max loved spending time with his best friend, Carmen. They played video games after school and shared everything with each other. One Friday, Carmen invited Max over for dinner at her house.
"You'll love it! My grandma is making paella, and she's the best cook!"
Max was excited, but he was also a little bit worried. He had never heard of paella. Max usually stuck to his favorite foods. It had taken days for his sister to get him to even try ice cream!

pieces.text: He imagined paella might be full of slimy vegetables or spicy sauces that would make his mouth burn.
Max wondered.

content.text: What if Carmen's family is upset? What if Carmen stops being my friend?

textContent.text: That evening, as Max walked to Carmen's house, he tried to think of a polite way to say, "No, thank you."

But when he arrived, Carmen's parents gave him a warm hug, and the house smelled delicious. The table was set with a big, steaming dish in the center. Inside was golden-brown rice with bits of chicken and colorful vegetables.
"My grandma's famous paella from Spain!" Carmen said proudly as everyone sat at the table. "She only makes it for special guests."

Max's heart beat wildly in his chest. The food looked different from anything he'd eaten before. He gulped nervously, and thought about how much Carmen's friendship meant to him. Max didn't want to hurt Carmen's feelings or seem rude.

pieces.text: The moment of truth had come. Max picked up his fork. He looked at Carmen, who was smiling. Then, he looked at the paella, which suddenly didn't seem so scary.
, Max thought.

content.text: If I try one bite, I can show Carmen I care about being her friend

textContent.text: With all the courage he could find, Max took a bite. He chewed the fluffy rice, the juicy chicken, and the sweet peppers.
To his surprise, it was delicious.
"Wow!" Max said, his eyes wide. "This is amazing!"
He took another bite, then another, and soon his plate was empty. Carmen laughed. "I told you my grandma was the best cook!"

textContent.text: Max loved spending time with his best friend, Carmen. They played video games after school and shared everything with each other. One Friday, Carmen invited Max over for dinner at her house.
"You'll love it! My grandma is making paella, and she's the best cook!"
Max was excited, but he was also a little bit worried. He had never heard of paella. Max usually stuck to his favorite foods. It had taken days for his sister to get him to even try ice cream!

pieces.text: He imagined paella might be full of slimy vegetables or spicy sauces that would make his mouth burn.
Max wondered.

content.text: What if Carmen's family is upset? What if Carmen stops being my friend?

textContent.text: That evening, as Max walked to Carmen's house, he tried to think of a polite way to say, "No, thank you."

But when he arrived, Carmen's parents gave him a warm hug, and the house smelled delicious. The table was set with a big, steaming dish in the center. Inside was golden-brown rice with bits of chicken and colorful vegetables.
"My grandma's famous paella from Spain!" Carmen said proudly as everyone sat at the table. "She only makes it for special guests."

Max's heart beat wildly in his chest. The food looked different from anything he'd eaten before. He gulped nervously, and thought about how much Carmen's friendship meant to him. Max didn't want to hurt Carmen's feelings or seem rude.

pieces.text: The moment of truth had come. Max picked up his fork. He looked at Carmen, who was smiling. Then, he looked at the paella, which suddenly didn't seem so scary.
, Max thought.

content.text: If I try one bite, I can show Carmen I care about being her friend

textContent.text: With all the courage he could find, Max took a bite. He chewed the fluffy rice, the juicy chicken, and the sweet peppers.
To his surprise, it was delicious.
"Wow!" Max said, his eyes wide. "This is amazing!"
He took another bite, then another, and soon his plate was empty. Carmen laughed. "I told you my grandma was the best cook!"

textContent.text: As Sarah and her mom strolled through downtown, the theater's bright new electric lamps drew their attention. Under the lights, Sarah noticed a shiny poster showing a woman with a stylish, ribbon-covered dress.
"The show is in town for one month only, just 25 cents!" Sarah read aloud. A smaller poster below added, "Tomorrow: tryouts for background actors!"
"Please, can we go?" Sarah begged, tugging on her mom's arm. Sarah had always dreamed of being an actress on the stage. When her mom finally agreed, Sarah knew she had to make a plan to stand out.

Back at home, she raced to her mom's sewing room. While her mom used a sewing machine at her dress shop in town, she didn't have one at home. Luckily, Mom had plenty of needles and thread for hand sewing.
Sarah began to snip and stitch colored fabrics that matched the poster at the theater. That night, she tossed and turned, anxious to catch the attention of the actors at tryouts.

But when she arrived at the theater, no one seemed to notice her in the eager crowd. She began to worry that her dress wouldn't be enough to make her stand out. Suddenly, a voice behind her said, "What a dress!"
She turned to see the main actress from the poster, tall and smiling. "Where did you get this dress?" the actress asked, her eyes wide.
"I made it," Sarah whispered, nearly fainting.
"Wow," said the actress, raising her eyebrows. "This dress is exactly something my character would wear! Could you make me one too?"

pieces.text: Sarah thought for a moment. Maybe she didn't have to be an actress. Maybe she could help
shine with her sewing.

textContent.text: "Really? Yes!" said Sarah.
So, instead of going on stage, Sarah got to work. She cut and sewed until she had the perfect dress. Before long, the other actors were asking her to make their costumes too.
On the day of the play, when the red velvet curtain came up, the crowd gasped. No one had ever seen such costumes. Best of all, Sarah got free tickets to every show!

Back at home, she raced to her mom's sewing room. While her mom used a sewing machine at her dress shop in town, she didn't have one at home. Luckily, Mom had plenty of needles and thread for hand sewing.
Sarah began to snip and stitch colored fabrics that matched the poster at the theater. That night, she tossed and turned, anxious to catch the attention of the actors at tryouts.

But when she arrived at the theater, no one seemed to notice her in the eager crowd. She began to worry that her dress wouldn't be enough to make her stand out. Suddenly, a voice behind her said, "What a dress!"
She turned to see the main actress from the poster, tall and smiling. "Where did you get this dress?" the actress asked, her eyes wide.
"I made it," Sarah whispered, nearly fainting.
"Wow," said the actress, raising her eyebrows. "This dress is exactly something my character would wear! Could you make me one too?"

pieces.text: Sarah thought for a moment. Maybe she didn't have to be an actress. Maybe she could help
shine with her sewing.

textContent.text: "Really? Yes!" said Sarah.
So, instead of going on stage, Sarah got to work. She cut and sewed until she had the perfect dress. Before long, the other actors were asking her to make their costumes too.
On the day of the play, when the red velvet curtain came up, the crowd gasped. No one had ever seen such costumes. Best of all, Sarah got free tickets to every show!

textContent.text: Oliver purred softly, snuggled up on his cozy blanket by the fireplace. Most cats spent their days chasing mice or climbing trees, but not Oliver. He belonged to Zinnia, the kindest witch in Willowdale. And he was perfectly content inside her cozy cabin, staring at the glow of the fire.
But one evening, a strange storm swept over Willowdale. Lightning flashed, thunder rumbled, and Oliver noticed Zinnia's crystal ball glowing on the table.

pieces.text: Curious, Oliver stretched out his nose to sniff it.
A spark shocked his nose.

textContent.text: "Ouch!" Oliver said. "I wish that silly ball of rock would just disappear."
Right before his eyes, the crystal faded away.

pieces.text: thought Oliver.

textContent.text: He had an idea. "I wish I had a big bowl of fish," he said. Suddenly, a bowl of fish appeared under his nose! Oliver purred with excitement.
For days, Oliver made wish after wish. He feasted on the best fish and batted around giant balls of yarn. But when news about his powers got out, animals began knocking on the cabin door nonstop.

pieces.text: Some animals asked for small favors, and Oliver was happy to help. But others weren't so kind. A crew of nosy bears from the
showed up asking endless questions. Some animals begged him to make them rich and powerful. Others even tried peeking through the cabin windows. It never stopped!

textContent.text: Oliver began to wonder whether his new powers were worth all the trouble.
One morning, a fox appeared with a strange-looking machine. "Mind if I zap you with this to study your powers?" she asked. "It will probably only hurt a little."
That was the final straw. Even endless bowls of fish weren't worth this. Oliver flicked his tail and told the fox to leave.
He knew what he had to do. "Here goes my last wish," he said. "I wish I didn't have these powers."
Immediately, Oliver felt different. But he wanted to be sure. "I wish I had a hundred gold pieces." To Oliver's great joy, nothing happened. "I wish I had another big plate of fish." Nothing.

pieces.text: Oliver let out a long sigh.

content.text: Now I can go back to being my old self

pieces.text: , he thought.

content.text: Magic is more trouble than it's worth

pieces.text: . Then, he curled up with his nose under his tail for a peaceful nap.

passage.text: Mark and Ivan sprinted down the block, racing each other from the school bus to Mark's house. Both boys had tried out for the Amity Elementary soccer team, and the results were supposed to be posted promptly at three o'clock. Dropping their backpacks by the door, the boys dashed to Mark's computer, where Mark logged on to the school website. The roster was up! He scrolled down, located his name, and pumped his fist. "Yes!" he cried with glee.

Ivan, who'd been peering over Mark's shoulder, didn't respond, and Mark turned to face him. The hurt, confused expression on Ivan's face caused Mark to spin back around. Scanning the roster, line by line, he searched for Ivan's name on the computer screen.
When he reached the end of the list, Mark felt like he'd been punched in the stomach. "This isn't fair," he sputtered.
Ivan just shrugged.

"Let's go back to school and talk to Coach Montgomery," Mark insisted. "Or I know—ask your parents to set up a conference with the principal. Maybe if Ms. Sanchez understands how much you want it, she'll make Coach give you another chance."
Shaking his head, Ivan shoved his hands in his pockets. "If I didn't make it, I didn't make it," he said gloomily.

Oh no, Mark thought. Is Ivan going to cry? Desperately, Mark changed his approach. "Amity doesn't know what it's doing," he said fiercely, pacing back and forth. "They've never reached the championship, or even the playoffs!"

Ivan stared silently at the computer screen, and Mark suddenly noticed his desktop's background was a photograph of the previous year's World Cup soccer champions. Mark hurried to shut down his computer so Ivan wouldn't have to look at it. Frustrated, Mark took a deep breath.
"At least you get to sleep in on Saturdays, instead of waking up early for practice," he told Ivan. "Right?"
No answer. Mark wished he could cheer people up the way Ivan could.

Even back in kindergarten, Ivan had been an expert at it; in fact, that was how they'd become friends in the first place. The first day of kindergarten, Mark had been horribly homesick, and he'd started crying during recess. It was so embarrassing! The other kids all attempted to comfort him, crowding around him and saying, "I'll push your swing!" "Want to hear a riddle?" "Don't cry!" But the chaotic swirl of shouts only made Mark feel more upset and alone. Eventually, the other kids drifted away, and only Ivan remained. He plunked down beside Mark, gently offering to keep him company until he felt better. Ten minutes later, they were having a swinging competition.
Remembering it now, Mark felt peaceful. For several minutes, he stayed silent, and then he said, "This must feel really awful."
Ivan finally turned away from the screen, looked at Mark, and nodded. "Yeah. It does."
Mark nodded. "We don't have to talk to Coach. We can just hang out until you feel better."

The friends sat in comfortable silence for a while. Then Ivan took a deep breath, wiped his eyes with his sweatshirt sleeve, and stood. "Let's go shoot some hoops," he suggested. "I'll probably feel better when I beat you." He grinned a little.
Mark stood, too. "You mean when I beat you," he replied. Ivan laughed, and they headed outside to the garage, where Mark grabbed the basketball. He flung it upward.
"Thanks," said Ivan, leaping to snatch the ball out of the air. He twirled it on his finger and glanced at Mark. "Seriously, thanks."

passage.text: On a Sunday afternoon, Claire and Zelda kicked up fall leaves as they walked to the library. "Brr!" Claire shivered, pulling her jacket tighter.
"That jacket doesn't look very warm," Zelda said.
Claire shrugged. "I like it. It's the same kind everyone else is wearing," she said.
Zelda rolled her eyes.
Claire admired Zelda's wild wooly cape, which perfectly reflected her best friend's unusual style. Then Claire coughed and added, "Not everyone loves to stand out the way you do."
Zelda just chuckled and pulled her cape tighter around her shoulders.
Claire turned to stomp on a crisp-looking leaf, but she suddenly became very dizzy. "I'm not feeling well, Zelda."
Zelda's arm was around her immediately. "You're burning up! Let's get you home right away."

Claire had caught the chicken pox. The next afternoon, she was bundled up in bed, wishing Zelda would come over, when her friend burst into her room waving an enormous bag. "I brought supplies," she said. "Your mom says you have to stay home for a week, but I can visit since I've already had the chicken pox."

Claire ducked under her blanket to hide the red bumps that covered her face. Zelda ignored Claire's sudden shyness and said, "Look what I brought— Matilda! This should keep your mind off the itching." Pulling Claire's favorite book out of her bag, Zelda adjusted the light and started reading aloud.
After a while, Zelda's voice got tired, so Claire read the next chapter to her. Zelda found her knitting needles and her bright-purple and lime-green yarn, and she knitted as she listened.
Every afternoon that week, Claire looked forward to Zelda's after-school visit. They read and chattered and played cards, and Zelda worked on her knitting.
By Saturday, Claire was able to get dressed and open the door for Zelda herself. But her face was still dotted with scabs.
Claire's mother said, "Won't it be lovely to go back to school on Monday?"
"No!" Claire shrieked, "I look terrible! Everyone will stare at me!"
"No they won't," Zelda said. "Everyone misses you, and they'll be glad to see you. Anyway, here." Zelda held out a gift-wrapped package.
"Thank you!" Claire cried. She ripped off the wrapping to find a gaudy purple-and-green sweater inside. She couldn't imagine wearing such bright, clashing colors. "Oh, did you make it?"
"I sure did! It might be my best one yet," Zelda said with a grin.
Seeing Zelda's hopeful face, Claire forced herself to put on a big smile. "It's beautiful," she lied.
"I thought it would make you feel better," Zelda said, "and maybe take people's attention away from your spots."
Claire nodded, dropping the sweater on a nearby table.
That night, Claire had nightmares of kids teasing her about her spotted face. In the morning, she called Zelda and said, "I can't go to school."
"Of course you can! Everyone will be nice, and it'll be fine. I'll meet you at the usual time."

Claire finally agreed. Hanging up the phone, she wished she could feel as strong and confident as Zelda usually did. Her glance fell on Zelda's purple-and-lime sweater, lying in a lump on the floor. What if Zelda was right—what if the sweater could keep people from noticing her face?
Claire smiled, scooped up the sweater and pulled it over her head. Of course, she thought, it's a perfect fit!

passage.text: Sammy's class was planning a field trip to the mountains to mine for gems. The day before the trip, Sammy kept telling his older brother about all the interesting rocks he thought he would find.
"I bet I'll find an arrowhead!" Sammy boasted to Leonard.
"Nobody finds arrowheads, just boring old rocks." Leonard laughed.
"Maybe people don't search carefully enough," Sammy replied.

The next day, Sammy sat with Samantha on the bus ride to the mountains. No one was surprised, since Sammy and Samantha were inseparable friends. They sat together in class, at lunch, and at recess. And they acted so alike that their teacher called them "Sams." "Settle down, Sams," Ms. Lee sometimes said.
Of course, Samantha agreed with Sammy that there would be arrowheads. The Sams decided that if either of them found an arrowhead, they would share it. They shook hands on the deal.

At the mine, a guide provided each student with a bucket of dirt and a tray with a bottom that looked like a window screen. "Pour your dirt onto your tray a little at a time," she said. "Rinse the dirt away with water from the creek to uncover the special rocks and gems."
Students started calling out their different discoveries. "Check out this sparkly silver stone!" "Dude, I got a tiger's-eye!"

Sammy uncovered a pinkish chunk of rose quartz, set it aside for safekeeping, and continued picking through the bits and pieces on his tray. Most of the others finished with their buckets and wandered off to explore an enormous sycamore tree nearby.

"Five more minutes," Ms. Lee called, as Sammy emptied the last pile of dirt from his bucket onto the tray. Leonard was right—no arrowheads. Sammy gave his tray a half-hearted shake. Suddenly a pointy black stone poked out of the pile—an arrowhead!
Where was Samantha? Had she noticed the arrowhead? Sammy spotted his friend climbing in the sycamore tree, and he slipped the arrowhead quickly into his pocket.

The class ate lunch under the tree. Sammy knew he should share his arrowhead with Samantha, but he kept it hidden. Meanwhile, Samantha seemed unusually quiet. Did she somehow know about his discovery?

Well, Sammy reminded himself, I discovered it on my own, and I don't have to share it just because of some silly deal. He bit into his cookie. It was his favorite butterscotch flavor, but at that moment, it tasted like sand.

Soon, the class started heading back to the bus. Sammy ducked behind a tree so that nobody could see, and he held his arrowhead out on his palm. As he was admiring its sparkle in the sunlight, Sammy spotted Samantha walking by herself. Sammy felt his chest tighten. He glanced at the arrowhead, but it wasn't glistening anymore. Clenching it in his fist, he hurried to catch up with the class.
Sammy sat in the empty seat next to Samantha. "I need to tell you something," he said.

But Samantha stuck out her fist, stopping him. "Me first," she said. Slowly, she turned over her fist and opened her fingers. Something small, black, and shiny rested on her palm—an arrowhead. "Sorry," Samantha whispered, her eyes lowered.
For a moment, Sammy didn't stir. Then he opened his own hand, and Samantha's mouth dropped open. They both started giggling, then laughing harder, until they had to gasp for air.
"Settle down, Sams," Ms. Lee said. "We have a long ride."

passage.text: Sammy's class was planning a field trip to the mountains to mine for gems. The day before the trip, Sammy kept telling his older brother about all the interesting rocks he thought he would find.
"I bet I'll find an arrowhead!" Sammy boasted to Leonard.
"Nobody finds arrowheads, just boring old rocks." Leonard laughed.
"Maybe people don't search carefully enough," Sammy replied.

The next day, Sammy sat with Samantha on the bus ride to the mountains. No one was surprised, since Sammy and Samantha were inseparable friends. They sat together in class, at lunch, and at recess. And they acted so alike that their teacher called them "Sams." "Settle down, Sams," Ms. Lee sometimes said.
Of course, Samantha agreed with Sammy that there would be arrowheads. The Sams decided that if either of them found an arrowhead, they would share it. They shook hands on the deal.

At the mine, a guide provided each student with a bucket of dirt and a tray with a bottom that looked like a window screen. "Pour your dirt onto your tray a little at a time," she said. "Rinse the dirt away with water from the creek to uncover the special rocks and gems."
Students started calling out their different discoveries. "Check out this sparkly silver stone!" "Dude, I got a tiger's-eye!"

Sammy uncovered a pinkish chunk of rose quartz, set it aside for safekeeping, and continued picking through the bits and pieces on his tray. Most of the others finished with their buckets and wandered off to explore an enormous sycamore tree nearby.

"Five more minutes," Ms. Lee called, as Sammy emptied the last pile of dirt from his bucket onto the tray. Leonard was right—no arrowheads. Sammy gave his tray a half-hearted shake. Suddenly a pointy black stone poked out of the pile—an arrowhead!
Where was Samantha? Had she noticed the arrowhead? Sammy spotted his friend climbing in the sycamore tree, and he slipped the arrowhead quickly into his pocket.

The class ate lunch under the tree. Sammy knew he should share his arrowhead with Samantha, but he kept it hidden. Meanwhile, Samantha seemed unusually quiet. Did she somehow know about his discovery?

Well, Sammy reminded himself, I discovered it on my own, and I don't have to share it just because of some silly deal. He bit into his cookie. It was his favorite butterscotch flavor, but at that moment, it tasted like sand.

Soon, the class started heading back to the bus. Sammy ducked behind a tree so that nobody could see, and he held his arrowhead out on his palm. As he was admiring its sparkle in the sunlight, Sammy spotted Samantha walking by herself. Sammy felt his chest tighten. He glanced at the arrowhead, but it wasn't glistening anymore. Clenching it in his fist, he hurried to catch up with the class.
Sammy sat in the empty seat next to Samantha. "I need to tell you something," he said.

But Samantha stuck out her fist, stopping him. "Me first," she said. Slowly, she turned over her fist and opened her fingers. Something small, black, and shiny rested on her palm—an arrowhead. "Sorry," Samantha whispered, her eyes lowered.
For a moment, Sammy didn't stir. Then he opened his own hand, and Samantha's mouth dropped open. They both started giggling, then laughing harder, until they had to gasp for air.
"Settle down, Sams," Ms. Lee said. "We have a long ride."

passage.text: Jenna stood at the refrigerator gulping milk straight from the bottle when Edward came in. Jenna wiped milk from her chin, asking, "Hey, where are you headed?"
"The Link," Edward answered, zipping his jacket. When Jenna looked at him blankly, he explained, "The Linkhart Art Museum, in the city."
"Oh, I love going to the city!" Jenna squeaked. "Can I come?"
Edward was silent for a moment and then said with a sigh, "Ask Dad."

Thirty minutes later, Edward and Jenna were settled into seats on the express train. Edward took out a book and started reading. Jenna tapped out rhythms on the armrests until she noticed Edward frowning and grinding his teeth. She switched to wiggling her knees and tapping her toes—quietly. She pulled a stick of gum from her pocket and offered it to Edward. Edward shook his head and kept reading.
When they pulled into Central Station, Jenna bounced on her toes, asking Edward, "Want to walk around and look for some street performers?"
"Nah, the Link's right here," Edward answered, steering them into the entrance of an enormous building. "Turn left. We're going to see the seventeenth-century Dutch art," he directed.

The Dutch section was full of dark paintings in fancy golden frames. Edward headed straight for a huge one in the corner. He stood there in front of the painting, just studying the art for several minutes. Jenna thought she should do the same. So she joined him by the picture, which showed an old woman holding a dull brown water pitcher.
"What's so great about this painting?" Jenna mumbled. She pondered for a while longer but came up with nothing.

Edward sighed and said, "Well, to begin with, observe how the artist handles the sunlight coming in from the window. And notice the shape and shading of this shadow on the chair…" His voice trailed off as he leaned closer to the painting.

Jenna shrugged and moved to another spot. All the other visitors appeared as excited as Edward, as if they were in on some secret that Jenna didn't know. She bounced and tried not to whistle as she circled the room. Finally, she told Edward they needed to find food immediately or she would faint from hunger. Edward groaned but herded her toward the museum snack bar. As they passed another long room on the way, Jenna caught a sudden glimpse of a sharp little squiggle painting. It looked as antsy as she felt. She stopped short, asking, "What's this section?"
Edward waved his hand, as if brushing aside an ant. "That's just modern art."

Jenna stepped closer to examine the painting that had captured her interest. The squiggle seemed somehow pent up—as if it wanted to race off the canvas, but it couldn't get free. Beside her, Edward shook his head. Then he asked, "Hey, do you like this art?"
"Yeah, I love it."
Edward's face broke into a wide smile. "Tell you what, then, Jenna. I'll head back to the seventeenth-century Dutch, and we'll meet right here in one hour. Then we'll find some lunch, okay?"
"Yep, sounds cool." Jenna figured chewing gum could prevent her from fainting for at least an hour. She pulled the pack of gum from her pocket and offered a stick to Edward.
Edward started to shake his head. Then he shrugged and held out his hand. "Sure," he said, "why not?"

passage.text: Briiiiing! Ari pressed the "off" button on the alarm clock and rolled out of bed. It was five o'clock in the morning, time to take care of the cows. Ari pulled on a pair of shorts and hurried outside.

At the barn, his classmate Daya was yawning and rubbing her eyes. Ari took a deep breath, enjoying the smell of fresh hay. Daya shook her head at him and complained, "I don't understand how you can smile so early in the morning."
Ari just laughed and grabbed a bucket to feed the animals.

Ari couldn't imagine life outside of his kibbutz, his farming community in rural Israel. Here he went to classes, did chores, and shared meals with his neighbors. In the summers, he and his friends camped and fished in wild places around the kibbutz.

After milking the cows, Ari ate a quick breakfast in the community center and then headed home to practice violin before school. He wanted to work on a difficult part of the music he'd be playing with the community band.

"Ari, my boy," said a familiar voice behind him. He looked around to see Mr. Elias, his music teacher, smiling. "I hear there may be some good news from the music school. You should be getting a letter soon."
"Morning, Mr. Elias! Thanks for the heads-up!"

Ari had been playing the violin for four years. His parents were surprised at his interest because they thought their son only liked sports. But Ari practiced violin every day. He had become such a fine player that Mr. Elias said there was nothing more that he could teach Ari.

Last month, Mr. Elias had taken Ari to audition for a music school in the city of Jerusalem, three hours away. The school was wonderful, and Ari had felt nervous playing for the teachers there. He didn't know whether he had played well enough to get in. But even worse, if he did get in, he didn't know what he'd do. Studying in Jerusalem would mean leaving home and living with his uncle in the city. How could he leave?

He remembered something his mother had said. "It's your decision. Even if you get into the school, you don't have to go," she had told him. "But you have a gift for music, and I'd love to see you use it." Ari hadn't decided yet, because he'd figured he wouldn't get in. But what did Mr. Elias mean about good news?

Back at home, Ari tried to focus on his practicing. Over and over, he landed the high note in the difficult part. He closed his eyes, imagining himself performing this piece on a large stage. The notes soared, the crowd clapped, and he bowed, soaking in the magic of the music.

Opening his eyes, he glanced out the window and spotted Daya walking to school, same as every day. Every day, everything is the same, he thought with a sigh. He remembered Mr. Elias telling him, "The music school is where you belong."

He opened the front door and almost ran into a man. It was a messenger holding a large envelope with Special Delivery stamped in red. Had the school accepted him? Ari's heart leaped, and suddenly he knew what he wanted.

passage.text: "Alexis will be here any minute, Mom!" Mariela called, coming into the living room.
Mariela's younger sister, Tina, stood on a chair, wearing a sparkly scarf and singing into a spatula. Tina stopped to ask, "Excited for your playdate?"
"It's not a playdate! It's a friend visiting," Mariela said.

Mom came in and held out her hand to Tina. "May I have your microphone, please?" she said, reaching for the spatula. "Mariela, I'm making brownies in case you and Alexis need to break the ice." Mom believed food had the power to make friendships grow.
"Brownies means it is a playdate!" Tina cried.
Mariela took a deep breath and replied, "Alexis is a new friend I just met. She hasn't had the chance to get to know us, so—"
"Want me to help?" Tina asked eagerly.

Mariela shuddered to imagine Tina shouting to Alexis, Me and Mariela love dressing up and playing ponies! Mariela told Tina, "Actually, it would be nice if you could be less silly. Maybe you could try to act more grown-up."
The doorbell rang, and Mariela ran to greet Alexis. When Mariela took a step back to let Alexis in, she almost knocked Tina over.
"Let's go upstairs, Alexis," Mariela said quickly, scooting around Tina.

The girls sat in Mariela's bedroom, and Mariela tried to think of things to talk about. They compared notes about middle school, which didn't take long. Then, they talked about movies. Then, they sat in silence. Mariela thought of Tina and her friend Frankie. Those two had so much to talk about that they often spoke at the same time. A heaviness settled in Mariela's chest.
Finally Mariela suggested, "I think my mom made brownies. Do you want some?"
"Sure," Alexis said, rising quickly.
In the kitchen, Tina was sitting at the table with an old leather briefcase. She nodded at Alexis, turned back to the briefcase, and snapped it closed. "Whew, that was a hard job," she said.
Mariela felt her face start to turn red as she grabbed two plates. Could she get Alexis safely back upstairs before Tina did something too silly?
Alexis was watching Tina. "You seem pretty busy," she told the younger girl.

"I certainly am," Tina answered as she rattled the briefcase, which seemed to contain her marble collection. "I'm a count-it," Tina continued. "I count things for my work, you know, and it's quite tiring, I must say." She sighed in a world-weary way and leaned back in her chair.
Alexis and Mariela met each other's eyes. Alexis's lips trembled as she held back a smile. "Does your mom work as an accountant?" she asked Mariela softly.
Mariela nodded. Tina gave the briefcase another rattle. Alexis covered her mouth with her hand as Mariela grinned and led her upstairs with the brownies.

Sitting and giggling on the bedroom floor, Alexis reached for a brownie. She grinned at Mariela, saying, "Your sister is so funny! I love it! She reminds me of my little brother. You wouldn't believe the absurd games he invents…"
Two hours flew by. When Alexis's father arrived to pick her up, the girls made plans to meet the next weekend.
Afterward, Mariela found Tina in the kitchen, sorting marbles. "So, how are the numbers looking, ma'am?" Mariela asked. She nodded seriously as Tina explained.

passage.text: A tall, slender man with short gray hair opened the heavy door of a tall glass office building and stepped into the sunlight. He wore a plain gray suit and dark sunglasses, as if he wanted to blend in.

The man glanced down at his watch. Suddenly he began running down the busy sidewalk. People hurried to step out of his way, some turning around to wonder why he was in such a rush. At the end of the block, the man bounded up a set of stairs and onto a small bridge.

Since it was nearly lunchtime, the bridge was swarming with people. With practiced skill, the man wove through the crowd of slowpokes at full speed. When he finally reached the opposite end of the bridge, he groaned. A large tour group had stopped in front of him. As soon as he managed to squeeze past them, he was off and running again.

He turned into a narrow alley, figuring he could save time by cutting across the city block. He briefly faltered when he came to a tipped-over garbage can blocking his path. Once he had found his balance, he was moving again. He easily hopped over the can, his jacket and tie flapping behind him.

Turning right, the man checked his watch again. He had just enough time, if everything went smoothly. He sped along the street and entered the small shop on the corner. Approaching the counter, he pointed to something in the window and asked the price.

The store clerk paused, looked up, put down her sandwich, and wiped a smudge of mayonnaise from her chin. She leafed through the catalog pages, running her fingers over each item. The man tapped his foot as the moments ticked by, until the clerk finally found the correct price. The clerk's eyes opened wide and her mouth dropped open when the man pulled a thick stack of bills from his wallet. But the man just counted them out, passed them over the counter, and tucked his purchase into his jacket pocket. Not waiting for a receipt, he coolly walked out of the store. Once outside the door, he broke into a jog again.

The Hotel Élégant was just ahead. At the sight of the uniformed doorman, the man slowed. He smoothed his hair with one hand and straightened his tie with the other as he strolled into the entrance hall. Breathing hard, he looked around the space, frowning. Then he spotted the brightly colored sign by a pair of double doors, and he pushed the doors open.
"Uncle Matthew!" Jake exclaimed. "You finally made it!"
"Happy Birthday, Jake!" Uncle Matthew said, giving Jake a quick hug.
"What took you so long this time?" Jake asked.

"I'm in time for the cake, aren't I? I had to stop to pick up your birthday present," Uncle Matthew said. He pulled the gold watch out of his jacket pocket and gave it to Jake. He winked at Jake, adding, "So that you never run late."

passage.text: Most of the animals at Shadowbrook Farm had been raised there. But Jasper the horse, Dora the cow, and Henrietta the chicken had all lived on other farms before they were taken to Shadowbrook. That's why they knew better than all the other animals how special Shadowbrook Farm was.

The farmer at Shadowbrook Farm loved her animals and showed it by giving them the best care possible. She organized the farm so that every animal slept well and had enough delicious food to eat. Jasper, Dora, and Henrietta trusted that their beloved farmer would always make the best choices to keep them all safe and happy.
That is, until she brought Webster into the picture.
Webster was a snow-white goose with a bright orange beak. At first, he didn't seem so bad. But then he opened his mouth.
Honk! Honk! Honk!
At first, Henrietta thought that Webster was just making noise because he was new and a little bit scared. But no, it quickly became clear that Webster just loved to honk.

Whenever new humans visited the farm, Webster honked at them. When Webster saw another bird in the sky, there it came—Honk! Honk! Honk! Pretty soon the farmer's golden retriever no longer liked to play in the lawn because Webster's honking upset him too much.
Henrietta paid a visit to her horse and cow friends to find out if she was the only one who found Webster to be extremely annoying. She wasn't.
"All this noise is giving me a headache," groaned Jasper.
"What good is it to have a goose?" grumbled Dora.
Jasper nodded in agreement. "Exactly! Every other animal here has a purpose. I give tourists rides on the nearby trails. Dora gives milk. And Henrietta provides eggs."
"But a goose doesn't give anyone rides or eggs or milk," concluded Henrietta. "So why do we need to have a goose here?"
Clucking to herself, Henrietta made her way back to the chicken coop. Then she looked out at the hill nearby, and her beak fell open in shock. On the top of the hill was a fox!
Henrietta hurried to warn the other chickens. But she knew it was no use. There was nothing to stop the fox from getting into the coop and hurting her and the other chickens.
Helpless, she watched the fox scurry down the hill, getting closer and closer. And then—
Honk! Honk! Honk!
Webster came out running and honking. With his wings spread open, he looked huge and frightening. The fox gave him one look, then ran away out of sight.
The chickens cheered.
"Thank you, Webster!" Henrietta told him. "Your honking sure came in handy today!"
"Of course," said Webster. "That's why I'm here—to protect you chickens!"
Henrietta smiled. She should have trusted that the wise farmer had a good reason to bring Webster to Shadowbrook.
Then she waddled back to the barn to tell Dora and Jasper that the new goose wasn't so bad after all.

passage.text: Most of the animals at Shadowbrook Farm had been raised there. But Jasper the horse, Dora the cow, and Henrietta the chicken had all lived on other farms before they were taken to Shadowbrook. That's why they knew better than all the other animals how special Shadowbrook Farm was.

The farmer at Shadowbrook Farm loved her animals and showed it by giving them the best care possible. She organized the farm so that every animal slept well and had enough delicious food to eat. Jasper, Dora, and Henrietta trusted that their beloved farmer would always make the best choices to keep them all safe and happy.
That is, until she brought Webster into the picture.
Webster was a snow-white goose with a bright orange beak. At first, he didn't seem so bad. But then he opened his mouth.
Honk! Honk! Honk!
At first, Henrietta thought that Webster was just making noise because he was new and a little bit scared. But no, it quickly became clear that Webster just loved to honk.

Whenever new humans visited the farm, Webster honked at them. When Webster saw another bird in the sky, there it came—Honk! Honk! Honk! Pretty soon the farmer's golden retriever no longer liked to play in the lawn because Webster's honking upset him too much.
Henrietta paid a visit to her horse and cow friends to find out if she was the only one who found Webster to be extremely annoying. She wasn't.
"All this noise is giving me a headache," groaned Jasper.
"What good is it to have a goose?" grumbled Dora.
Jasper nodded in agreement. "Exactly! Every other animal here has a purpose. I give tourists rides on the nearby trails. Dora gives milk. And Henrietta provides eggs."
"But a goose doesn't give anyone rides or eggs or milk," concluded Henrietta. "So why do we need to have a goose here?"
Clucking to herself, Henrietta made her way back to the chicken coop. Then she looked out at the hill nearby, and her beak fell open in shock. On the top of the hill was a fox!
Henrietta hurried to warn the other chickens. But she knew it was no use. There was nothing to stop the fox from getting into the coop and hurting her and the other chickens.
Helpless, she watched the fox scurry down the hill, getting closer and closer. And then—
Honk! Honk! Honk!
Webster came out running and honking. With his wings spread open, he looked huge and frightening. The fox gave him one look, then ran away out of sight.
The chickens cheered.
"Thank you, Webster!" Henrietta told him. "Your honking sure came in handy today!"
"Of course," said Webster. "That's why I'm here—to protect you chickens!"
Henrietta smiled. She should have trusted that the wise farmer had a good reason to bring Webster to Shadowbrook.
Then she waddled back to the barn to tell Dora and Jasper that the new goose wasn't so bad after all.

passage.text: I wiped the frost from the window and peered outside. The sun shone brightly, sending sparkling prisms through the icicles hanging from the slate roof. Grandfather's rusty pickup truck sat empty. It was ready to be loaded up with my homemade hot cocoa mix. Tomorrow, the truck would carry them down the mountain. I turned to Grandmother, who was measuring careful scoops of my cocoa mix into jars.
"Do we have enough?" I asked, surveying the rows of jars. Silver ribbons were coiled nearby.
"Enough for what, Marie?" said Grandmother. "The winter festival or an army?"
"I just want to be sure!" I said, smiling. "Enough for everyone to try a cup before—"
"Before they vote for their favorite booth, yes," Grandmother finished.
She smiled kindly, but I felt a tiny sliver of doubt in my chest. I imagined crowds of people ignoring my small table. Instead, everyone would rush to taste pastries and tea from a fancier booth.
"Do you think maybe I made too much? What if no one wants to try it?" I asked.

"No. Every jar will be gone," Grandmother said as she wiped her hands on her apron. She then wrapped me in an enormous hug and whispered, "Your hot cocoa is going to win first place tomorrow. You've worked very hard, and it's delicious. Now, get these ribbons on just the way you want. Then I'll pack the jars up so they won't break in the truck."
The next morning, I could hear the steady rush of wind even from under my thick quilt. I got out of bed and opened the curtains.

Our yard was gone, blanketed with fresh snow and ice. A snowdrift nearly covered the shed across the yard. I saw an enormous tree limb lying across Grandfather's truck. A group of people from the town, along with Grandfather, were trying to move it. One man chopped away at it with an ax, which looked tiny next to the giant limb.
I felt Grandmother enter the room behind me.
"Marie—" she said.
"Is the winter festival still happening?" I asked.

"Maybe. They say it's not that bad down the mountain. Those men and women from the town came to help. But there's still all the snow on the main roads. I don't think there's any way for you to get there," she said gently.
Tears filled my eyes as I watched the ax making tiny cuts in the enormous branch. I felt like all of my work had been for nothing. Then a rich smell reached me from the kitchen.
"Is that bacon?" I asked.
"Yes, I'm cooking breakfast for everyone who's helping," answered Grandmother.
I wiped my eyes. "I think they could use some of my hot cocoa, too."
Grandmother smiled at me. "I can't think of a better treat for all that hard work."
"I'll get the jars," I said.
Grandmother squeezed my shoulder. "I'll start heating up the milk," she said.

contents.text: A story summary includes the most important details in a story. To write a good summary, think about the main story elements.

The story's background includes information that sets the scene and introduces the main characters. It may also state the story's setting or describe an important event that happens at the beginning of the story.
The main problem in the story is something that goes wrong for the characters, or something that needs to be fixed or changed. The problem, or conflict, is what causes the characters to take action.
The solution to the story's main problem is how the problem in the story is solved. The solution, or resolution, is what wraps up the story.

You can take notes on story elements using a graphic organizer, like a table. Then, you can use the graphic organizer to help you write a story summary. Your summary should include the story elements. You should also include transition words and a few more details to help the summary flow.

contents.text: Lily is babysitting her little sister Marly while their parents go out. During dinner, Lily gets upset because Marly spills spaghetti all over the kitchen floor. However, Lily has an idea. She attaches rags to her and Marly's feet, and they twirl across the kitchen floor. Just like that, cleaning up the kitchen turns into a fun game.

passage.text: Danny paces in front of the library doors, counting the bricks. A few other kids are talking while they wait. He doesn't look at them, though. He's busy thinking about his strategy. Empty the box, find the edges, sort the colors.
Finally, Mrs. McMillan unlocks the doors.
"Puzzlers, head into the back room," she says. "We'll get started shortly."
Inside the room, Danny sees rows of tables topped with beautiful, unopened jigsaw puzzle boxes. A banner hangs on the wall: "A Piece of the Earth: County Jigsaw Puzzle Tournament."

Danny wanders the rows, looking at the puzzles. Each box has a picture more beautiful than the last: toucans crouched in tropical trees, elephants stampeding across a plain, a seascape with towering cliffs and foaming waves.

Danny has always loved doing jigsaw puzzles with his grandmother. To him, there is nothing more satisfying than snapping puzzle pieces together. In a puzzle, there is an answer for everything, and every piece has its place.

Danny has been practicing for the puzzle tournament for weeks. He started completing bigger and bigger puzzles on his own and timing himself. He's pretty sure he can work quickly enough to win today—especially if he sticks to the plan. Empty. Edges. Colors.
As the room fills with puzzlers, Danny stops in front of a puzzle: a farm in a cornfield, with a setting sun tinting the clouds like stained glass.
"Any puzzle you want, Danny," says Mrs. McMillan. "They're all the same number of pieces."
"I have a good feeling about this one," Danny whispers, grinning.
"Great," she says. "Have a seat. Then we'll get you some teammates."
Danny stares at her, confused.
"Each table works as a team," Mrs. McMillan explains with a smile. "No one could possibly do such a large puzzle on their own in one afternoon!"
Danny feels a wave of dread as three kids sit down at his table. He has no way of winning now. They don't have a system. They're only going to slow him down.
The starting bell rings. The boy across from Danny opens the box and dumps the pieces out.
Before anyone can reach for the pieces, Danny blurts out, "What if we each take a color?"
The two other kids shrug and agree. The boy across from Danny looks alarmed.
"You mean…after we do the edge pieces, right?" he asks.
Danny smiles.
"Of course. How about if you sort out the edges while the three of us split up the colors? I bet we'll be faster that way," Danny offers.
The four kids lean over the table to spread out the pieces. The room fills with the steady hum of voices and the snapping of hundreds of tiny puzzle pieces.

passage.text: A splash of liquid. The crinkle of leaves being crushed.
Alayna and Francie slipped on their goggles, and Francie stirred the mess using a large wooden spoon.

It was warm and sunny, perfect for working in the science lab. Alayna and Francie's lab was under some lilac bushes at the edge of the woods. The bushes kept their bottles, beakers, and science books safe. While Francie stirred, Alayna glanced at the flyer speared on a branch overhead: "Science Fair This Weekend! Open for Entries Now."
"No change yet," said Francie, still stirring.
Alayna sighed, opened her notebook, and wrote down the results.
"Don't worry," said Francie. "We'll come up with something good for the science fair."
"I hope so. I feel like we've tested every leaf in this forest," said Alayna.
"Um, Alayna?" said Francie, putting down the spoon.
Both girls peered into the glass bowl. The liquid had turned into a thick blue goo, and the goo was—
"Why is it moving? Are you shaking the bowl?" asked Alayna.
"I'm not even touching it," Francie said in a hushed voice.

Suddenly the gooey mass started sliding up the side of the bowl. Alayna and Francie watched wide-eyed as the goo scrunched and stretched, scrunched and stretched, crawling like an inchworm to escape the bowl. It landed in the dirt, paused for a moment, then crawled quickly toward the opening in the bushes. Before the girls knew it, the goo was gone.
"Come on!" said Alayna, grabbing the bowl and her backpack. "We have to catch it!"

They ran out of their lab and followed the faint but steady sound of crunching leaves. The blue goo was heading deeper into the woods, crawling so quickly that the girls had to jog. Alayna ran ahead and plopped the glass bowl on top of the goo.
But the bowl kept sliding along until Alayna stepped on it. Francie tore a sheet of paper from her notebook and slid it under the bowl.
"This is how my mom carries spiders out of the house," Francie explained. "Though we might want to tape the paper to the bowl, so the goo can't slip out."
"Good idea!" Alayna exclaimed, pulling a roll of tape out of her backpack. "Then we can bring it to the science fair! Or maybe…"
"Maybe what?"
"Maybe we shouldn't bring it to the fair right away. It really seems to want to get somewhere," said Alayna. "See, it's all pressed up against one side of the bowl. It wants to go that way."
The two girls watched as the goo scrunched itself against the glass.
"Well. It would make sense to find out where it was headed," admitted Francie. "For science."
"Let's carry it around for a bit and see where it takes us. Then we'll have better results for the fair, right?" said Alayna.
Alayna finished taping up the bowl and handed it to Francie. She pulled her notebook and a pencil out of her backpack. Then the girls began to march through the woods, following the goo's directions.

The bushes kept their bottles, beakers, and science books safe. While Francie stirred, Alayna glanced at the flyer speared on a branch overhead: "Science Fair This Weekend! Open for Entries Now."
"No change yet," said Francie, still stirring.
Alayna sighed, opened her notebook, and wrote down the results.
"Don't worry," said Francie. "We'll come up with something good for the science fair."
"I hope so. I feel like we've tested every leaf in this forest," said Alayna.
"Um, Alayna?" said Francie, putting down the spoon.
Both girls peered into the glass bowl. The liquid had turned into a thick blue goo, and the goo was—
"Why is it moving? Are you shaking the bowl?" asked Alayna.
"I'm not even touching it," Francie said in a hushed voice.

Suddenly the gooey mass started sliding up the side of the bowl. Alayna and Francie watched wide-eyed as the goo scrunched and stretched, scrunched and stretched, crawling like an inchworm to escape the bowl. It landed in the dirt, paused for a moment, then crawled quickly toward the opening in the bushes. Before the girls knew it, the goo was gone.
"Come on!" said Alayna, grabbing the bowl and her backpack. "We have to catch it!"

They ran out of their lab and followed the faint but steady sound of crunching leaves. The blue goo was heading deeper into the woods, crawling so quickly that the girls had to jog. Alayna ran ahead and plopped the glass bowl on top of the goo.
But the bowl kept sliding along until Alayna stepped on it. Francie tore a sheet of paper from her notebook and slid it under the bowl.
"This is how my mom carries spiders out of the house," Francie explained. "Though we might want to tape the paper to the bowl, so the goo can't slip out."
"Good idea!" Alayna exclaimed, pulling a roll of tape out of her backpack. "Then we can bring it to the science fair! Or maybe…"
"Maybe what?"
"Maybe we shouldn't bring it to the fair right away. It really seems to want to get somewhere," said Alayna. "See, it's all pressed up against one side of the bowl. It wants to go that way."
The two girls watched as the goo scrunched itself against the glass.
"Well. It would make sense to find out where it was headed," admitted Francie. "For science."
"Let's carry it around for a bit and see where it takes us. Then we'll have better results for the fair, right?" said Alayna.
Alayna finished taping up the bowl and handed it to Francie. She pulled her notebook and a pencil out of her backpack. Then the girls began to march through the woods, following the goo's directions.

passage.text: Covered from head to toe in sunscreen, I stood at the edge of the water next to my kayak, trying to look relaxed. I figured I would just watch my two older cousins, Ira and Eddie, and do whatever they did. Kayaking can't be that hard, I told myself. People do it all the time.
"All right, let's get going," Eddie said. "I'm so ready for lunch."

The three of us were kayaking to a small, secluded beach to meet everyone else for a picnic lunch. This picnic was part of our yearly family vacation. Most people were driving, but Ira and Eddie wanted to kayak. I couldn't believe they asked me to come. Of course I said yes—even though I'd never been kayaking before.

We headed across the bay towards a mangrove swamp. Kayaking was a lot of work, especially once the wind picked up. It felt like I was paddling through sludge. No, wet cement. Wet cement that was starting to dry.

Entering the swamp was a relief. The wind disappeared, and the mangrove trees shielded us from the sun. We paddled through a tunnel created by the twisting trunks. Their knotty branches curved around our path.

However, the tunnel soon became narrower. The nose of my kayak kept getting stuck in tree roots, and then I would have to push it out again using my paddle. I couldn't make it more than a few feet without getting trapped.
"All good, Neil?" Eddie called over his shoulder.
"Yeah, all good. Just checking out some shells," I replied, trying to sound calm. If I was slow and careful, I could catch up to them without them knowing how much trouble I was having.

Eddie and Ira's voices got fainter as they paddled farther ahead of me. Frantic, I gave a huge push with the paddle, which completely wedged my kayak between two tree trunks. I tried to push myself free again, but the kayak wouldn't move an inch.
Eventually, I heard Ira's voice getting closer. "Neil? Are you okay?"
"Yeah, I'm fine," I sputtered. "I just…I found this cool turtle."
Ira paddled back toward me and glanced at my stuck kayak.
"The turtle's gone now," I said.
"Sorry I missed it," he said. "Here, let me give you a hand."
He pushed the front of my kayak out of the trees.
"Why don't you go ahead of me, and I can show you a few things?" Ira offered.

He explained how I didn't need to grip the paddle so tightly, and he showed me how to gently guide my boat through the tunnel with my hand on the trees. We stopped a few times to look at cool fish in the water.

I felt much more comfortable kayaking by the time we exited the mangrove swamp. We soon reached a small white beach, where our family was setting up picnic blankets. Ira and I hopped out of our kayaks and pulled them onto the sand.
"Where'd you guys go?" asked Eddie.
"Oh, Neil found a cool turtle," said Ira, giving me a quick grin.
I smiled back at him and found a spot next to my cousins for lunch.

passage.text: Covered from head to toe in sunscreen, I stood at the edge of the water next to my kayak, trying to look relaxed. I figured I would just watch my two older cousins, Ira and Eddie, and do whatever they did. Kayaking can't be that hard, I told myself. People do it all the time.
"All right, let's get going," Eddie said. "I'm so ready for lunch."

The three of us were kayaking to a small, secluded beach to meet everyone else for a picnic lunch. This picnic was part of our yearly family vacation. Most people were driving, but Ira and Eddie wanted to kayak. I couldn't believe they asked me to come. Of course I said yes—even though I'd never been kayaking before.

We headed across the bay towards a mangrove swamp. Kayaking was a lot of work, especially once the wind picked up. It felt like I was paddling through sludge. No, wet cement. Wet cement that was starting to dry.

Entering the swamp was a relief. The wind disappeared, and the mangrove trees shielded us from the sun. We paddled through a tunnel created by the twisting trunks. Their knotty branches curved around our path.

However, the tunnel soon became narrower. The nose of my kayak kept getting stuck in tree roots, and then I would have to push it out again using my paddle. I couldn't make it more than a few feet without getting trapped.
"All good, Neil?" Eddie called over his shoulder.
"Yeah, all good. Just checking out some shells," I replied, trying to sound calm. If I was slow and careful, I could catch up to them without them knowing how much trouble I was having.

Eddie and Ira's voices got fainter as they paddled farther ahead of me. Frantic, I gave a huge push with the paddle, which completely wedged my kayak between two tree trunks. I tried to push myself free again, but the kayak wouldn't move an inch.
Eventually, I heard Ira's voice getting closer. "Neil? Are you okay?"
"Yeah, I'm fine," I sputtered. "I just…I found this cool turtle."
Ira paddled back toward me and glanced at my stuck kayak.
"The turtle's gone now," I said.
"Sorry I missed it," he said. "Here, let me give you a hand."
He pushed the front of my kayak out of the trees.
"Why don't you go ahead of me, and I can show you a few things?" Ira offered.

He explained how I didn't need to grip the paddle so tightly, and he showed me how to gently guide my boat through the tunnel with my hand on the trees. We stopped a few times to look at cool fish in the water.

I felt much more comfortable kayaking by the time we exited the mangrove swamp. We soon reached a small white beach, where our family was setting up picnic blankets. Ira and I hopped out of our kayaks and pulled them onto the sand.
"Where'd you guys go?" asked Eddie.
"Oh, Neil found a cool turtle," said Ira, giving me a quick grin.
I smiled back at him and found a spot next to my cousins for lunch.

passage.text: "What's that you're looking at?" I asked Uncle Keith while I munched on my cereal. He was flipping through a handful of old photos.

"Your Aunt Phyllis found some photos. Look, it's me at Bluebird Commons back in the old days," Uncle Keith said. After Uncle Keith married Aunt Phyllis, they moved back to the same building that Uncle Keith had lived in as a kid. I joined them eight years ago.
I looked at the photo and laughed. It was strange to see a young Uncle Keith playing baseball in the same courtyard where I now played with my friends.
"What was Bluebird Commons like back then?" I asked between bites. "Has it changed a lot?"
"Oh, yes. You should have seen the courtyard, Jeremy," said Uncle Keith. He glanced out our apartment window. The courtyard had a rotted wooden bench and a faded sign by the entrance.

"It was beautiful. Everyone gathered every so often to clean up, take care of the plants, and just talk like neighbors," he sighed. "Now I hate having to walk through that courtyard. It's just a sad place."
"No one has time to clean the place up now," Aunt Phyllis chimed in from the other room. "It's all rush, rush, rush. Speaking of which, Jer—"

"Yeah, I'm going!" I said, grabbing my backpack and running out the door. Even though I needed to hurry, I paused for a moment in the courtyard. I tried to see it how Uncle Keith once saw it. Mostly I just saw broken bricks, peeling paint, and food wrappers blowing in the biting February wind. Then, looking closer, I saw something else.
"Jer, what are you doing?" asked my neighbor Nisha, who had just run outside. "Come on, we'll be late."
We sprinted to the bus stop. All the other Bluebird Commons kids were already there. We talked and joked the whole way to school, but my mind was turning over and over.
"Are you guys free this weekend?" I asked the group. "I need help with a surprise for my aunt and uncle." Then I told them my idea.
On Saturday evening, I stood by the bus stop, waiting for my aunt and uncle to come back from their friend's house.
"Well, hello there, Jer!" Aunt Phyllis called as she got off the bus. "How nice of you to greet us. Is everything okay?"
"Everything's okay! Everything is great. Come on!" I said. I grabbed Uncle Keith's bag and led them toward Bluebird Commons.
When the full courtyard came into view, they both gasped. Most of the kids from our building were there, hard at work. The trash was nearly gone, and my friends were collecting stray food wrappers.
"You did all of this?" my uncle asked. He looked toward the apartment steps, where Nisha was painting a cheerful bluebird onto a sign.
"We all did," I answered. "And we're not done! Every Saturday, we're going to work on something new: a garden, fresh paint, new benches where all the neighbors can sit and talk…"

passage.text: In the cold, foggy forest, Nathan hiked ahead of his older sister Willa. He was sure that Willa knew these mysterious woods better than he did. She had been exploring them for years before Nathan was old enough to join her. Still, he wanted to show her that he could find his way on his own. All at once, a strong gust of wind picked up, startling him. Nathan slipped on the fallen leaves, lost his balance, and hit the ground with a thump.

After a moment, Nathan sat up, struggling to catch his breath. As he brushed the dust off his body, he noticed a big blue feather floating down from the sky. He examined the feather closely, so closely he barely saw its owner glide silently down from above. But at the last minute, he looked up and found himself face-to-face with a large dragon covered in blue feathers.

They stared silently at each other. Then, the dragon folded its silky wings and came closer. Its razor-sharp teeth were just inches from Nathan's face. With a puff of smoke, the dragon let out a sharp screech, and Nathan screamed back.
The dragon took flight as Nathan leaped to his feet and scurried in the opposite direction. Running blindly through the thick fog, he bumped into something, knocking it backward.
Through the fog, Nathan saw Willa get to her feet and brush herself off.
"I'm sorry," Nathan apologized, "I didn't see you there."
"Why were you running? Did something scare you again?"

"Ah, no…I just like stretching my legs, that's all," Nathan lied, embarrassed. He was always trying to prove that he wasn't a baby. And he definitely didn't want Willa to think he was making up stories about a feathery dragon.
Willa snickered. "Come on, let's get moving. I'm freezing!"

On their way back, Nathan and Willa stopped in their tracks at the sight of a dark, swooping shadow. Standing before them was the blue dragon, puffing smoke and baring its sharp teeth. Nathan jumped and let out a shout, cowering behind Willa.
Willa laughed. "Scared of dragons? Don't worry, Buttercup won't bite. I've known her for years."
Willa pulled a cookie from her pocket and tossed it to the dragon. Buttercup caught it and swallowed it whole. Willa placed a cookie into Nathan's trembling hand.
"Now you try it."
Nathan gulped, but Willa encouraged him with a nod. He slowly moved from behind her and stuck out his hand.

With a gentle slurp, the dragon gobbled up the cookie from Nathan's hand. Nathan relaxed, wiping the dragon's slobber on his shirt. Buttercup shook her feathery wings and excitedly ran in circles around him.
"She likes you!" Willa cried.
Nathan cracked a smile, running his hands over Buttercup's soft blue feathers.
"Yeah, she does! I'm not scared of dragons," Nathan boasted.
"In that case, why don't we hitch a ride back to the house?"
Willa hopped onto Buttercup's back, grabbed Nathan's wrist, and pulled him up with her.
"Are you ready for your first dragon ride, Nathan?"
Before he could answer, Buttercup took to the air, carrying the two of them high above the fog.
